# tokio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tokio/^1/

## Expand description

A runtime for writing reliable network applications without compromising speed.

Tokio is an event-driven, non-blocking I/O platform for writing asynchronous applications with the Rust programming language. At a high level, it provides a few major components:

- Tools for [working with asynchronous tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks), including[synchronization primitives and channels](https://docs.rs/sync/index.html)and[timeouts, sleeps, and intervals](https://docs.rs/time/index.html).
- APIs for [performing asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-io), including[TCP and UDP](https://docs.rs/net/index.html)sockets,[filesystem](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html)operations, and[process](https://docs.rs/process/index.html)and[signal](https://docs.rs/signal/index.html)management.
- A [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)for executing asynchronous code, including a task scheduler, an I/O driver backed by the operating system’s event queue (`epoll`,`kqueue`,`IOCP`, etc…), and a high performance timer.

Guide level documentation is found on the [website](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial).

[§](https://docs.rs#a-tour-of-tokio)A Tour of Tokio

Tokio consists of a number of modules that provide a range of functionality essential for implementing asynchronous applications in Rust. In this section, we will take a brief tour of Tokio, summarizing the major APIs and their uses.

The easiest way to get started is to enable all features. Do this by
enabling the `full` feature flag:

`tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#authoring-applications)Authoring applications

Tokio is great for writing applications and most users in this case shouldn’t
worry too much about what features they should pick. If you’re unsure, we suggest
going with `full` to ensure that you don’t run into any road blocks while you’re
building your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example shows the quickest way to get started with Tokio.

`tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#authoring-libraries)Authoring libraries

As a library author your goal should be to provide the lightest weight crate that is based on Tokio. To achieve this you should ensure that you only enable the features you need. This allows users to pick up your crate without having to enable unnecessary features.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

This example shows how you may want to import features for a library that just
needs to `tokio::spawn` and use a `TcpStream`.

`tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt", "net"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks)Working With Tasks

Asynchronous programs in Rust are based around lightweight, non-blocking
units of execution called [ tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks). The

[module provides important tools for working with tasks:](https://docs.rs/task/index.html)

`tokio::task`- The `spawn``JoinHandle`
- Functions for [running blocking operations](https://docs.rs/task/index.html#blocking-and-yielding)in an asynchronous task context.

The [ tokio::task](https://docs.rs/task/index.html) module is present only when the “rt” feature flag
is enabled.

The [ tokio::sync](https://docs.rs/sync/index.html) module contains synchronization primitives to use when
needing to communicate or share data. These include:

- channels (`oneshot``mpsc``watch``broadcast`
- a non-blocking `Mutex`
- an asynchronous `Barrier`

The `tokio::sync` module is present only when the “sync” feature flag is
enabled.

The [ tokio::time](https://docs.rs/time/index.html) module provides utilities for tracking time and
scheduling work. This includes functions for setting

[timeouts](https://docs.rs/time/fn.timeout.html)for tasks,

[sleeping](https://docs.rs/time/fn.sleep.html)work to run in the future, or

[repeating an operation at an interval](https://docs.rs/time/fn.interval.html).

In order to use `tokio::time`, the “time” feature flag must be enabled.

Finally, Tokio provides a *runtime* for executing asynchronous tasks. Most
applications can use the [ #[tokio::main]](https://docs.rs/attr.main.html) macro to run their code on the
Tokio runtime. However, this macro provides only basic configuration options. As
an alternative, the

[module provides more powerful APIs for configuring and managing runtimes. You should use that module if the](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)

`tokio::runtime``#[tokio::main]` macro doesn’t
provide the functionality you need.Using the runtime requires the “rt” or “rt-multi-thread” feature flags, to
enable the current-thread [single-threaded scheduler](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#current-thread-scheduler) and the [multi-thread
scheduler](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#multi-thread-scheduler), respectively. See the [ runtime module
documentation](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#runtime-scheduler) for details. In addition, the “macros” feature
flag enables the

`#[tokio::main]` and `#[tokio::test]` attributes.[§](https://docs.rs#cpu-bound-tasks-and-blocking-code)CPU-bound tasks and blocking code

Tokio is able to concurrently run many tasks on a few threads by repeatedly
swapping the currently running task on each thread. However, this kind of
swapping can only happen at `.await` points, so code that spends a long time
without reaching an `.await` will prevent other tasks from running. To
combat this, Tokio provides two kinds of threads: Core threads and blocking threads.

The core threads are where all asynchronous code runs, and Tokio will by default
spawn one for each CPU core. You can use the environment variable `TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS`
to override the default value.

The blocking threads are spawned on demand, can be used to run blocking code
that would otherwise block other tasks from running and are kept alive when
not used for a certain amount of time which can be configured with [ thread_keep_alive](https://docs.rs/runtime/struct.Builder.html#method.thread_keep_alive).
Since it is not possible for Tokio to swap out blocking tasks, like it
can do with asynchronous code, the upper limit on the number of blocking
threads is very large. These limits can be configured on the

[.](https://docs.rs/runtime/struct.Builder.html)

`Builder`To spawn a blocking task, you should use the [ spawn_blocking](https://docs.rs/task/fn.spawn_blocking.html) function.

```
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // This is running on a core thread.
    let blocking_task = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| {
        // This is running on a blocking thread.
        // Blocking here is ok.
    });
    // We can wait for the blocking task like this:
    // If the blocking task panics, the unwrap below will propagate the
    // panic.
    blocking_task.await.unwrap();
}
```
If your code is CPU-bound and you wish to limit the number of threads used
to run it, you should use a separate thread pool dedicated to CPU bound tasks.
For example, you could consider using the [rayon](https://docs.rs/rayon) library for CPU-bound
tasks. It is also possible to create an extra Tokio runtime dedicated to
CPU-bound tasks, but if you do this, you should be careful that the extra
runtime runs *only* CPU-bound tasks, as IO-bound tasks on that runtime
will behave poorly.

Hint: If using rayon, you can use a [ oneshot](https://docs.rs/sync/oneshot/index.html) channel to send the result back
to Tokio when the rayon task finishes.

[§](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-io)Asynchronous IO

As well as scheduling and running tasks, Tokio provides everything you need to perform input and output asynchronously.

The [ tokio::io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) module provides Tokio’s asynchronous core I/O primitives,
the

[,](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncRead.html)

`AsyncRead`[, and](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncWrite.html)

`AsyncWrite`[traits. In addition, when the “io-util” feature flag is enabled, it also provides combinators and functions for working with these traits, forming as an asynchronous counterpart to](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncBufRead.html)

`AsyncBufRead`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/index.html)

`std::io`Tokio also includes APIs for performing various kinds of I/O and interacting with the operating system asynchronously. These include:

- `tokio::net`- [TCP](https://docs.rs/net/tcp/index.html),- [UDP](https://docs.rs/net/struct.UdpSocket.html), and- [Unix Domain Sockets](https://docs.rs/net/unix/index.html)(enabled by the “net” feature flag),
- `tokio::fs`- `std::fs`
- `tokio::signal`
- `tokio::process`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

A simple TCP echo server:

```
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
use tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?;
    loop {
        let (mut socket, _) = listener.accept().await?;
        tokio::spawn(async move {
            let mut buf = [0; 1024];
            // In a loop, read data from the socket and write the data back.
            loop {
                let n = match socket.read(&mut buf).await {
                    // socket closed
                    Ok(0) => return,
                    Ok(n) => n,
                    Err(e) => {
                        eprintln!("failed to read from socket; err = {:?}", e);
                        return;
                    }
                };
                // Write the data back
                if let Err(e) = socket.write_all(&buf[0..n]).await {
                    eprintln!("failed to write to socket; err = {:?}", e);
                    return;
                }
            }
        });
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

Tokio uses a set of [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) to reduce the amount of compiled code. It
is possible to just enable certain features over others. By default, Tokio
does not enable any features but allows one to enable a subset for their use
case. Below is a list of the available feature flags. You may also notice
above each function, struct and trait there is listed one or more feature flags
that are required for that item to be used. If you are new to Tokio it is
recommended that you use the `full` feature flag which will enable all public APIs.
Beware though that this will pull in many extra dependencies that you may not
need.

- `full`: Enables all features listed below except- `test-util`and unstable features.
- `rt`: Enables- `tokio::spawn`, the current-thread scheduler, and non-scheduler utilities.
- `rt-multi-thread`: Enables the heavier, multi-threaded, work-stealing scheduler.
- `io-util`: Enables the IO based- `Ext`traits.
- `io-std`: Enable- `Stdout`,- `Stdin`and- `Stderr`types.
- `net`: Enables- `tokio::net`types such as- `TcpStream`,- `UnixStream`and- `UdpSocket`, as well as (on Unix-like systems)- `AsyncFd`and (on FreeBSD)- `PollAio`.
- `time`: Enables- `tokio::time`types and allows the schedulers to enable the built-in timer.
- `process`: Enables- `tokio::process`types.
- `macros`: Enables- `#[tokio::main]`and- `#[tokio::test]`macros.
- `sync`: Enables all- `tokio::sync`types.
- `signal`: Enables all- `tokio::signal`types.
- `fs`: Enables- `tokio::fs`types.
- `test-util`: Enables testing based infrastructure for the Tokio runtime.
- `parking_lot`: As a potential optimization, use the- `parking_lot`- `const`context.- `MSRV`may increase according to the- `parking_lot`

*Note:  AsyncRead and AsyncWrite traits do not require any features and are
always available.*

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

Some feature flags are only available when specifying the `tokio_unstable` flag:

- `tracing`: Enables tracing events.
- `io-uring`: Enables- `io-uring`(Linux only).
- `taskdump`: Enables- `taskdump`(Linux only).

Likewise, this flag enables access to unstable APIs.

This flag enables **unstable** features. The public API of these features
may break in 1.x releases. To enable these features, the `--cfg tokio_unstable` argument must be passed to `rustc` when compiling. This
serves to explicitly opt-in to features which may break semver conventions,
since Cargo [does not yet directly support such opt-ins](https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/feature-request-unstable-opt-in-non-transitive-crate-features/16193#why-not-a-crate-feature-2).

You can specify it in your project’s `.cargo/config.toml` file:

```
[build]
rustflags = ["--cfg", "tokio_unstable"]
```
`[build]` section does **not**go in a

`Cargo.toml` file. Instead it must be placed in the Cargo config
file `.cargo/config.toml`.
Alternatively, you can specify it with an environment variable:

```
## Many *nix shells:
export RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable"
cargo build
```
```
## Windows PowerShell:
$Env:RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable"
cargo build
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-platforms)Supported platforms

Tokio currently guarantees support for the following platforms:

- Linux
- Windows
- Android (API level 21)
- macOS
- iOS
- FreeBSD

Tokio will continue to support these platforms in the future. However, future releases may change requirements such as the minimum required libc version on Linux, the API level on Android, or the supported FreeBSD release.

Beyond the above platforms, Tokio is intended to work on all platforms
supported by the mio crate. You can find a longer list [in mio’s
documentation](https://crates.io/crates/mio#platforms). However, these additional platforms may
become unsupported in the future.

Note that Wine is considered to be a different platform from Windows. See mio’s documentation for more information on Wine support.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm-support)`WASM` support

Tokio has some limited support for the `WASM` platform. Without the
`tokio_unstable` flag, the following features are supported:

- `sync`
- `macros`
- `io-util`
- `rt`
- `time`

Enabling any other feature (including `full`) will cause a compilation
failure.

The `time` module will only work on `WASM` platforms that have support for
timers (e.g. wasm32-wasi). The timing functions will panic if used on a `WASM`
platform that does not support timers.

Note also that if the runtime becomes indefinitely idle, it will panic immediately instead of blocking forever. On platforms that don’t support time, this means that the runtime can never be idle in any way.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-wasm-support)Unstable `WASM` support

Tokio also has unstable support for some additional `WASM` features. This
requires the use of the `tokio_unstable` flag.

Using this flag enables the use of `tokio::net` on the wasm32-wasi target.
However, not all methods are available on the networking types as `WASI`
currently does not support the creation of new sockets from within `WASM`.
Because of this, sockets must currently be created via the `FromRawFd`
trait.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use task::`- [spawn](https://docs.rs/task/fn.spawn.html);- `rt`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [doc](https://docs.rs/doc/index.html)- `docsrs`and Unix
- Types which are documented locally in the Tokio crate, but does not actually live here.
- [fs](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html)- `fs`
- Asynchronous file utilities.
- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)
- Traits, helpers, and type definitions for asynchronous I/O functionality.
- [net](https://docs.rs/net/index.html)
- TCP/UDP/Unix bindings for `tokio`.
- [process](https://docs.rs/process/index.html)- `process`
- An implementation of asynchronous process management for Tokio.
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)- `rt`
- The Tokio runtime.
- [signal](https://docs.rs/signal/index.html)- `signal`
- Asynchronous signal handling for Tokio.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)
- Due to the `Stream`trait’s inclusion in`std`landing later than Tokio’s 1.0 release, most of the Tokio stream utilities have been moved into the`tokio-stream`
- [sync](https://docs.rs/sync/index.html)- `sync`
- Synchronization primitives for use in asynchronous contexts.
- [task](https://docs.rs/task/index.html)- `rt`
- Asynchronous green-threads.
- [time](https://docs.rs/time/index.html)- `time`
- Utilities for tracking time.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `macros`
- Waits on multiple concurrent branches, returning when **all**branches complete.
- [pin](https://docs.rs/macro.pin.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `macros`
- Waits on multiple concurrent branches, returning when the **first**branch completes, cancelling the remaining branches.
- [task_](https://docs.rs/macro.task_local.html)- local - `rt`
- Declares a new task-local key of type `tokio::task::LocalKey`
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `macros`
- Waits on multiple concurrent branches, returning when **all**branches complete with`Ok(_)`or on the first`Err(_)`.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [main](https://docs.rs/attr.main.html)- `rt`and- `macros`
- Marks async function to be executed by the selected runtime. This macro
helps set up a `Runtime`without requiring the user to use[Runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/struct.Runtime.html)or[Builder](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/struct.Builder.html)directly.
- [test](https://docs.rs/attr.test.html)- `rt`and- `macros`
- Marks async function to be executed by runtime, suitable to test environment.
This macro helps set up a `Runtime`without requiring the user to use[Runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/struct.Runtime.html)or[Builder](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/struct.Builder.html)directly.

# kigumi_mod_base - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/kigumi-mod-base/1.0.0/target-redirect/kigumi_mod_base/

## Expand description

Base module: the foundational models other modules build on — currency, partner (contacts), and company. Root of the dependency graph (no dependencies of its own).

Multi-company: `res.company` is the unit of data isolation; transactional models carry a
`company_id` (added per model, e.g. sale.order). Partners are shared (no company_id) to avoid a
circular FK with res.company; company-specific contacts can be modelled later behind a deferred
FK. The active-company filtering rule lives in the security layer (Ctx.company + a record rule).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [seed](https://docs.rs/seed/index.html)
- Base reference data, run by the `register_seed!`seam at every migrate while`base`is installed: one default currency + company (multi-company needs a company to exist), a starter country set, and the read-only`res.groups`projection of every registered ACL/rule group. Every block is guarded by an exists-check — the DB is the authority, an operator change is never overwritten. Relocated verbatim from kigumi-cli so adopter binaries get it too.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [IrAttachment](https://docs.rs/struct.IrAttachment.html)
- [ResCompany](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCompany.html)
- [ResCountry](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCountry.html)
- [ResCountry](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCountryState.html)- State
- [ResCurrency](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCurrency.html)
- [ResCurrency](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCurrencyRate.html)- Rate
- [ResGroups](https://docs.rs/struct.ResGroups.html)
- [ResPartner](https://docs.rs/struct.ResPartner.html)
- [ResUsers](https://docs.rs/struct.ResUsers.html)

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [ACLS](https://docs.rs/static.ACLS.html)
- Base ACLs: the everyday `user`group reads the foundational reference data and the group list; the user directory (`res.users`) is admin-only (read-only — account changes go through auth).`ir.attachment`generic CRUD is admin-only: end users reach files through the gated`/attachments`endpoints (which check host access and run elevated), never the raw model.
- [MANIFEST](https://docs.rs/static.MANIFEST.html)
- Module manifest. `base`depends on nothing and anchors the catalog.

---

# kigumi_mod_base::seed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-mod-base/1.0.0/kigumi_mod_base/seed/index.html

## Expand description

Base reference data, run by the `register_seed!` seam at every migrate while `base` is
installed: one default currency + company (multi-company needs a company to exist), a starter
country set, and the read-only `res.groups` projection of every registered ACL/rule group.
Every block is guarded by an exists-check — the DB is the authority, an operator change is
never overwritten. Relocated verbatim from kigumi-cli so adopter binaries get it too.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [seed_](https://docs.rs/fn.seed_base_data.html)- base_ - data
- Seeds one default currency + company on a fresh instance, plus countries and groups.

---

# ACLS in kigumi_mod_base - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-mod-base/1.0.0/kigumi_mod_base/static.ACLS.html

`pub static ACLS: &[`[Acl](https://docs.rs/kigumi-core/0.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/kigumi_core/security/struct.Acl.html)]## Expand description

Base ACLs: the everyday `user` group reads the foundational reference data and the group list;
the user directory (`res.users`) is admin-only (read-only — account changes go through auth).
`ir.attachment` generic CRUD is admin-only: end users reach files through the gated `/attachments`
endpoints (which check host access and run elevated), never the raw model.

---

Module manifest. `base` depends on nothing and anchors the catalog.

# sim_kernel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

sim-kernel is the small protocol kernel of the SIM Rust runtime.

The kernel defines contracts; libraries supply behavior. This crate holds
the protocol and contract types – forms, values, stores, registry and
callable surfaces, the [ shape](https://docs.rs/shape/index.html) protocol, evaluation policy, and the ABI
transport – while concrete behavior (parsers, number domains, the standard
distribution, and server/agent/browse implementations) lives in separate
library crates loaded against these contracts. SIM is a Rust runtime, not a
Lisp runtime; Lisp is one codec surface among several.

The one deliberate exception is the pair of built-in *reference backends*:
[ list::VecList](https://docs.rs/list/struct.VecList.html) (a

[) and](https://docs.rs/list/trait.ListValue.html)

`list::ListValue`[(a](https://docs.rs/table/struct.AssocTable.html)

`table::AssocTable`[). These are the kernel’s bootstrap list and table implementations – minimal, correct, and self-annotated](https://docs.rs/table/trait.Table.html)

`table::Table``sim-non-citizen` –
so the runtime can stand up collections before any library loads. They are
reference implementations, not the only backends: alternatives load as libs
against the [/](https://docs.rs/list/trait.ListBackend.html)

`list::ListBackend`[contracts. (Future cleanup: move even these into a default-loaded distribution lib so the kernel ships pure contracts; tracked against the constellation reorg.)](https://docs.rs/table/trait.TableBackend.html)

`table::TableBackend`The kernel data flow is:

`tokens -> checked forms -> objects -> checked calls -> objects -> encoded forms`[§](https://docs.rs#module-map)Module map

# sim_lib_numbers_codec - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-numbers-codec/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

The number-literal codec surface: helpers that build the `numeric-plugin-v1`
descriptor symbols and table values advertising a numeric codec or method
provider to the runtime.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [numeric_](https://docs.rs/fn.numeric_plugin_descriptor_symbol.html)- plugin_ - descriptor_ - symbol
- Build the descriptor symbol `group/name`advertising a numeric codec or method provider under the`numeric-plugin-v1`API.
- [numeric_](https://docs.rs/fn.numeric_plugin_descriptor_value.html)- plugin_ - descriptor_ - value
- Build the `numeric-plugin-v1`descriptor table for`method`, recording its plugin`kind`, whether it is`adaptive`, and the`provider`domain that supplies it.

# sim_lib_numbers_f64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-numbers-f64/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

The `numbers/f64` domain: double-precision floating-point literals and
values, their scalar arithmetic, and promotion into `complex`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [F64Number](https://docs.rs/struct.F64NumberDomain.html)- Domain
- The double-precision 64-bit floating-point number domain: parses decimal
literals and declares the promotion edge into `complex`
- [F64Numbers](https://docs.rs/struct.F64NumbersLib.html)- Lib
- The library that installs the `numbers/f64`domain: its literal class and shapes, value shape, scalar ops, and promotion rules.

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [RECIPES](https://docs.rs/static.RECIPES.html)
- The cookbook recipes embedded for the `numbers/f64`domain, packaged at build time for runtime help and browse surfaces.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [number_](https://docs.rs/fn.number_domain.html)- domain
- The `numbers/f64`domain symbol shared by this crate’s literals, values, and ops.

# sim_lib_numbers_func - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-numbers-func/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

Function number domain: callable function values built over CAS or native
bodies, with `fn`, `call`, and `grad` operations for the `Func` domain.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Func](https://docs.rs/struct.Func.html)
- A callable function value in the `Func`number domain: its bound variables plus an optional symbolic (CAS) body and/or native body.
- [Func](https://docs.rs/struct.FuncMetadata.html)- Metadata
- Out-of-band annotations attached to a `Func`
- [Func](https://docs.rs/struct.FuncNumbersLib.html)- Numbers - Lib
- Library that installs the `Func`number domain: its domain object, value class and shape, the`fn`/`call`/`grad`callables, and the promotion rules that lift scalar number values into constant functions.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [call_](https://docs.rs/fn.call_symbol.html)- symbol
- Returns the symbol bound to the `call`apply-a-function callable.
- [fn_](https://docs.rs/fn.fn_symbol.html)- symbol
- Returns the symbol bound to the `fn`function-builder callable.
- [func_](https://docs.rs/fn.func_class_symbol.html)- class_ - symbol
- Returns the class symbol for the constructible `Func`value class (`numbers/Func`).
- [func_](https://docs.rs/fn.func_domain_symbol.html)- domain_ - symbol
- Returns the domain symbol that names the `Func`number domain (`numbers/func`).
- [grad_](https://docs.rs/fn.grad_symbol.html)- symbol
- Returns the symbol bound to the `grad`gradient-of-a-function callable.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Native](https://docs.rs/type.NativeFn.html)- Fn
- A native (Rust-backed) function body: a closure invoked with the runtime
context and the evaluated argument values, used when a `Func`has no CAS body.

---

# sim_lib_numbers_numeric - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-numbers-numeric/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

Numeric evaluation surface: the `numeric` domain exposes `numeric-diff`,
`integrate`, `ode-solve`, and composed pipelines over a registry of pluggable
differentiator, quadrature, and ODE-solver backends.

A composed pipeline pairs a [ sim_lib_numbers_func::Func](https://docs.rs/sim-lib-numbers-func/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_lib_numbers_func/implementation/value/struct.Func.html) with a numeric
domain such as quadrature or ODE solving, a method such as

`simpson` or
`rk4`, and a state kind. The resulting [is a first-class runtime value that can be inspected and run through](https://docs.rs/struct.ComposedPipeline.html)

`ComposedPipeline``numeric/run-composed`.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Composed](https://docs.rs/struct.ComposedPipeline.html)- Pipeline
- First-class value describing a numeric pipeline composition.
- [Diff](https://docs.rs/struct.DiffOpts.html)- Opts
- Options controlling a numeric-differentiation call.
- [Numeric](https://docs.rs/struct.NumericNumbersLib.html)- Numbers - Lib
- Library that installs the numeric evaluation surface: the `numeric-diff`,`integrate`,`integrate-adapt`,`ode-solve`,`numeric/compose`, and`numeric/run-composed`callables that dispatch to the registered numeric backends.
- [OdeOpts](https://docs.rs/struct.OdeOpts.html)
- Options controlling an ODE-solve call.
- [OdeProblem](https://docs.rs/struct.OdeProblem.html)
- A first-order initial-value ODE problem `dy/dx = f(x, y)`handed to an`OdeSolver`
- [Quad](https://docs.rs/struct.QuadOpts.html)- Opts
- Options controlling an integration (quadrature) call.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Numeric](https://docs.rs/enum.NumericKind.html)- Kind
- The category of numeric backend, used to route a plugin to the right slot in the registry.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/enum.PipelineKind.html)- Kind
- Numeric pipeline domain selected for a composed pipeline.
- [State](https://docs.rs/enum.StateKind.html)- Kind
- Runtime state representation selected for a composed pipeline.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Differentiator](https://docs.rs/trait.Differentiator.html)
- A numeric differentiation backend: computes `df/dvar`at a point.
- [Numeric](https://docs.rs/trait.NumericPlugin.html)- Plugin
- Common interface for every numeric backend plugin: it reports its method name and the kind of operation it implements.
- [OdeSolver](https://docs.rs/trait.OdeSolver.html)
- A numeric ODE-solving backend: integrates an initial-value problem.
- [Quadrature](https://docs.rs/trait.Quadrature.html)
- A numeric integration (quadrature) backend: computes a definite integral.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [global_](https://docs.rs/fn.global_numeric_registry.html)- numeric_ - registry
- Returns the process-global numeric registry, creating it on first access.
- [integrate_](https://docs.rs/fn.integrate_adapt_symbol.html)- adapt_ - symbol
- Returns the symbol bound to the adaptive `integrate-adapt`operation.
- [integrate_](https://docs.rs/fn.integrate_symbol.html)- symbol
- Returns the symbol bound to the fixed-rule `integrate`operation.

# RkNumbersLib in sim_lib_numbers_rk - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-numbers-rk/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_numbers_rk/struct.RkNumbersLib.html

`pub struct RkNumbersLib;`## Expand description

Registered numeric plugin library that installs this crate’s Runge-Kutta ODE-solver backends.

Loading this [ Lib](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/library/loaders/trait.Lib.html) registers the fixed-step solvers (forward Euler,
backward Euler, midpoint, classic RK4) and the adaptive Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg
(RKF45) integrator as

`ode-solve` plugins on the numeric surface, and
installs the plugin descriptor values that advertise each backend to the
registry.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use sim_kernel::Lib;
use sim_lib_numbers_rk::RkNumbersLib;
let lib = RkNumbersLib::new();
let manifest = lib.manifest();
// One descriptor export per registered solver (4 fixed-step plus RKF45).
assert_eq!(manifest.exports.len(), 5);
```

# capnp-rpc 0.26.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnp-rpc/0.26.1

# capnp-rpc-rust

This is a [level one](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features)
implementation of the Cap'n Proto remote procedure call protocol.
It is a fairly direct translation of the original
[C++ implementation](https://github.com/sandstorm-io/capnproto).

## Defining an interface

First, make sure that the
[ capnp executable](https://capnproto.org/capnp-tool.html)
is installed on your system,
and that you have the

[crate in the](https://crates.io/crates/capnpc)

`capnpc``build-dependencies` section of your `Cargo.toml`.
Then, in a file named `foo.capnp`, define your interface:```
@0xa7ed6c5c8a98ca40;
interface Bar {
    baz @0 (x :Int32) -> (y :Int32);
}
interface Qux {
    quux @0 (bar :Bar) -> (y :Int32);
}
```
Now you can invoke the schema compiler in a
[ build.rs](http://doc.crates.io/build-script.html) file, like this:

```
```
Such a command generates a `foo_capnp.rs` file in the `OUT_DIR`
directory provided by `cargo`.

To import the generated code, add a line like this at the root of your crate:

`generated_code!`(If you want to import the code at a non-toplevel module location, then you will
need to use the `$Rust.parentModule` annotation, defined in `rust.capnp`.)

## Calling methods on an RPC object

For each defined interface, the generated code includes a `Client` struct
that can be used to call the interface's methods. For example, the following
code calls the `Bar.baz()` method:

```
```
A `bar::Client` is a reference to a possibly-remote `Bar` object.
The Cap'n Proto RPC runtime tracks the number of such references
that are live at any given time and automatically drops the
object when none are left.

## Implementing an interface

The generated code also includes a `Server` trait for each of your interfaces.
To create an RPC-enabled object, you must implement that trait.

```
```
Then you can convert your object into a capability client like this:

```
let client: Client = new_client;
```
This new `client` can now be sent across the network.
You can use it as the bootstrap capability when you construct an `RpcSystem`,
and you can pass it in RPC method arguments and results.

## Async methods

The methods of the generated `Server` traits return
a value of type `impl Future<Output = Result<(), ::capnp::Error>>`.
As you have seen above,
these can be implented as `async fn` methods returning `Result<(), ::capnp::Error>`.

The RPC response will be sent back to the method's caller once two things have happened:

- The `Results`struct has been dropped.
- The method's returned `Future`has resolved.

Usually (1) happens before (2).

Here's an example of a method implementation that does not return immediately because it awaits another request:

```
```
It's possible for multiple calls of `quux()` to be active at the same time
on the same object, and they do not need to return in the same order
as they were called.

## Further reading

- The [hello world example](https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/examples/hello-world)demonstrates a basic request/reply pattern.
- The [calculator example](https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator)demonstrates how to use[promise pipelining](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#time-travel-promise-pipelining).
- The [pubsub example](https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/examples/pubsub)shows how even an interface with no methods can be useful.
- The [Sandstorm raw API example app](https://github.com/dwrensha/sandstorm-rawapi-example-rust)shows how Sandstorm lets you write web apps using Cap'n Proto instead of HTTP.

---

# capnp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp/^0.26.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#capn-proto-runtime-library)Cap’n Proto Runtime Library

This crate contains basic facilities for reading and writing
[Cap’n Proto](https://capnproto.org) messages in Rust. It is intended to
be used in conjunction with code generated by the
[capnpc-rust](https://crates.io/crates/capnpc) crate.

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3.0/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use futures_core::future::`- [Future](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Future.html);
- `pub use futures_core::future::`- [TryFuture](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.TryFuture.html);
- `pub use futures_util::future::`- [FutureExt](https://docs.rs/future/trait.FutureExt.html);
- `pub use futures_util::future::`- [TryFutureExt](https://docs.rs/future/trait.TryFutureExt.html);
- `pub use futures_core::stream::`- [Stream](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Stream.html);
- `pub use futures_core::stream::`- [TryStream](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.TryStream.html);
- `pub use futures_util::stream::`- [StreamExt](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.StreamExt.html);
- `pub use futures_util::stream::`- [TryStreamExt](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.TryStreamExt.html);

- `pub use futures_util::sink::`- [SinkExt](https://docs.rs/sink/trait.SinkExt.html);

- `pub use futures_io::`- [AsyncRead](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.AsyncRead.html);- `std`
- `pub use futures_io::`- [AsyncSeek](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.AsyncSeek.html);- `std`
- `pub use futures_io::`- [AsyncWrite](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.AsyncWrite.html);- `std`
- `pub use futures_util::`- [AsyncBufReadExt](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncBufReadExt.html);- `std`
- `pub use futures_util::`- [AsyncReadExt](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncReadExt.html);- `std`

- `pub use futures_util::`- [AsyncWriteExt](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncWriteExt.html);- `std`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [channel](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html)- `alloc`
- Asynchronous channels.
- [compat](https://docs.rs/compat/index.html)- `compat`
- Interop between `futures`0.1 and 0.3.

- Built-in executors and related tools.

- Asynchronous values.

- Asynchronous I/O.
- [lock](https://docs.rs/lock/index.html)- `alloc`
- Futures-powered synchronization primitives.

- This module contains the `Never`type.

- A “prelude” for crates using the `futures`crate.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

# capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/target-redirect/capnp_rpc/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [Cap’n Proto remote procedure call](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html)
protocol. Includes all [Level 1](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
# Cap'n Proto schema
interface Foo {
    identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust server defining an implementation of Foo.
struct FooImpl;
impl foo::Server for FooImpl {
    async fn identity(
        self: Rc<Self>,
        params: foo::IdentityParams,
        mut results: foo::IdentityResults
    ) -> Result<(), ::capnp::Error> {
        let x = params.get()?.get_x();
        results.get().set_y(x);
        Ok(())
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust client calling a remote implementation of Foo.
let mut request = foo_client.identity_request();
request.get().set_x(123);
let promise = request.send().promise.and_then(|response| {
    println!("results = {}", response.get()?.get_y());
    Ok(())
});
```
For a more complete example, see [https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [rpc_](https://docs.rs/rpc_capnp/index.html)- capnp
- Code generated from
[rpc.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/rpc.capnp).
- [rpc_](https://docs.rs/rpc_twoparty_capnp/index.html)- twoparty_ - capnp
- Code generated from
[rpc-twoparty.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/rpc-twoparty.capnp).
- [twoparty](https://docs.rs/twoparty/index.html)
- An implementation of `VatNetwork`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [pry](https://docs.rs/macro.pry.html)
- Like `try!()``Promise<T, E>``Result<T, E>`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Capability](https://docs.rs/struct.CapabilityServerSet.html)- Server - Set
- Collection of unwrappable capabilities.
- [Disconnector](https://docs.rs/struct.Disconnector.html)
- A `Future`that can be run to disconnect an`RpcSystem`’s ConnectionState and wait for it to be closed.
- [Imbued](https://docs.rs/struct.ImbuedMessageBuilder.html)- Message - Builder
- [RpcSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.RpcSystem.html)
- A portal to objects available on the network.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Connection](https://docs.rs/trait.Connection.html)
- A two-way RPC connection.
- [Flow](https://docs.rs/trait.FlowController.html)- Controller
- Tracks a particular RPC stream in order to implement a flow control algorithm.
- [Incoming](https://docs.rs/trait.IncomingMessage.html)- Message
- A message received from a `VatNetwork`
- [Outgoing](https://docs.rs/trait.OutgoingMessage.html)- Message
- A message to be sent by a `VatNetwork`
- [SetTarget](https://docs.rs/trait.SetTarget.html)
- Trait implemented by the reconnecting client to set new connection out-of-band.
- [VatNetwork](https://docs.rs/trait.VatNetwork.html)
- Network facility between vats, it determines how to form connections between vats.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [auto_](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_reconnect.html)- reconnect
- Creates a new client that reconnects when getting `ErrorKind::Disconnected`
- [lazy_](https://docs.rs/fn.lazy_auto_reconnect.html)- auto_ - reconnect
- Creates a new client that lazily connect and also reconnects when getting `ErrorKind::Disconnected`
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_client.html)- client
- Creates a new local RPC client of type `C`out of an object that implements a server trait`S`.
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_client_from_rc.html)- client_ - from_ - rc
- Variant of `new_client`that works on an`Rc<S>`.
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_future_client.html)- future_ - client
- Creates a `Client`from a future that resolves to a`Client`.

## Expand description

An implementation of the [Cap’n Proto remote procedure call](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html)
protocol. Includes all [Level 1](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
# Cap'n Proto schema
interface Foo {
    identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);

```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```

    async fn identity(
        self: Rc<Self>,
        params: foo::IdentityParams,
        mut results: foo::IdentityResults
    ) -> Result<(), ::capnp::Error> {
        let x = params.get()?.get_x();
        results.get().set_y(x);
        Ok(())
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```

For a more complete example, see [https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator)

[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! An implementation of the [Cap'n Proto remote procedure call](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html)
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! protocol. Includes all [Level 1](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! # Example
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! ```capnp
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! # Cap'n Proto schema
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! interface Foo {
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!     identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! }
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! ```
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! ```ignore
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! // Rust server defining an implementation of Foo.
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! struct FooImpl;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! impl foo::Server for FooImpl {
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!     async fn identity(
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!         self: Rc<Self>,
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!         params: foo::IdentityParams,
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!         mut results: foo::IdentityResults
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     ) -> Result<(), ::capnp::Error> {
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!         let x = params.get()?.get_x();
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!         results.get().set_y(x);
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!         Ok(())
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!     }
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! }
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! ```
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! ```ignore
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! // Rust client calling a remote implementation of Foo.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! let mut request = foo_client.identity_request();
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! request.get().set_x(123);
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! let promise = request.send().promise.and_then(|response| {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!     println!("results = {}", response.get()?.get_y());
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!     Ok(())
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! });
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! ```
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! For a more complete example, see <https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator>
[60](https://docs.rs#60)

[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// Like [`try!()`], but for functions that return a [`Promise<T, E>`] rather than a [`Result<T, E>`].
[85](https://docs.rs#85)///
[86](https://docs.rs#86)/// Unwraps a `Result<T, E>`. In the case of an error `Err(e)`, immediately returns from the
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// enclosing function with `Promise::err(e)`.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)#[macro_export]
[89](https://docs.rs#89)macro_rules! pry {
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    ($expr:expr) => {
[91](https://docs.rs#91)        match $expr {
[92](https://docs.rs#92)            ::std::result::Result::Ok(val) => val,
[93](https://docs.rs#93)            ::std::result::Result::Err(err) => {
[94](https://docs.rs#94)                return ::capnp::capability::Promise::err(::std::convert::From::from(err))
[95](https://docs.rs#95)            }
[96](https://docs.rs#96)        }
[97](https://docs.rs#97)    };
[98](https://docs.rs#98)}

[112](https://docs.rs#112)use capnp::message;
[113](https://docs.rs#113)
[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// A message to be sent by a [`VatNetwork`].
[115](https://docs.rs#115)pub trait OutgoingMessage {
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    /// Gets the message body, which the caller may fill in any way it wants.
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    ///
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    /// The standard RPC implementation initializes it as a Message as defined
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    /// in `schema/rpc.capnp`.
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    fn get_body(&mut self) -> ::capnp::Result<::capnp::any_pointer::Builder<'_>>;
[121](https://docs.rs#121)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// Same as `get_body()`, but returns the corresponding reader type.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    fn get_body_as_reader(&self) -> ::capnp::Result<::capnp::any_pointer::Reader<'_>>;
[124](https://docs.rs#124)
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// Sends the message. Returns a promise that resolves once the send has completed.
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// Dropping the returned promise does *not* cancel the send.
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    fn send(
[128](https://docs.rs#128)        self: Box<Self>,
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    ) -> (
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        Promise<(), Error>,
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        Rc<message::Builder<message::HeapAllocator>>,
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    );
[133](https://docs.rs#133)
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    /// Takes the inner message out of `self`.
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    fn take(self: Box<Self>) -> ::capnp::message::Builder<::capnp::message::HeapAllocator>;
[136](https://docs.rs#136)
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    /// Gets the total size of the message, for flow control purposes. Although the caller
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    /// could also call get_body().target_size(), doing that would walk the message tree,
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// whereas typical implementations can compute the size more cheaply by summing
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    /// segment sizes.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    fn size_in_words(&self) -> usize;
[142](https://docs.rs#142)}
[143](https://docs.rs#143)
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// A message received from a [`VatNetwork`].
[145](https://docs.rs#145)pub trait IncomingMessage {
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    /// Gets the message body, to be interpreted by the caller.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    ///
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    /// The standard RPC implementation interprets it as a Message as defined
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    /// in `schema/rpc.capnp`.
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    fn get_body(&self) -> ::capnp::Result<::capnp::any_pointer::Reader<'_>>;
[151](https://docs.rs#151)}
[152](https://docs.rs#152)
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// A two-way RPC connection.
[154](https://docs.rs#154)///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// A connection can be created by [`VatNetwork::connect()`].
[156](https://docs.rs#156)pub trait Connection<VatId> {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    /// Returns the connected vat's authenticated VatId.  It is the VatNetwork's
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    /// responsibility to authenticate this, so that the caller can be assured
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    /// that they are really talking to the identified vat and not an imposter.
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    fn get_peer_vat_id(&self) -> VatId;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    /// Allocates a new message to be sent on this connection.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    ///
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    /// If `first_segment_word_size` is non-zero, it should be treated as a
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// hint suggesting how large to make the first segment.  This is entirely
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    /// a hint and the connection may adjust it up or down.  If it is zero,
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    /// the connection should choose the size itself.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    fn new_outgoing_message(&mut self, first_segment_word_size: u32) -> Box<dyn OutgoingMessage>;
[169](https://docs.rs#169)
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// Waits for a message to be received and returns it.  If the read stream cleanly terminates,
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// returns None. If any other problem occurs, returns an Error.
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    fn receive_incoming_message(&mut self) -> Promise<Option<Box<dyn IncomingMessage>>, Error>;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    /// Constructs a flow controller for a new stream on this connection.
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    ///
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// Returns (fc, p), where fc is the new flow controller and p is a promise
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    /// that must be polled in order to drive the flow controller.
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    fn new_stream(&mut self) -> (Box<dyn FlowController>, Promise<(), Error>) {
[179](https://docs.rs#179)        let (fc, f) = crate::flow_control::FixedWindowFlowController::new(
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            crate::flow_control::DEFAULT_WINDOW_SIZE,
[181](https://docs.rs#181)        );
[182](https://docs.rs#182)        (Box::new(fc), f)
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    }
[184](https://docs.rs#184)
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// Waits until all outgoing messages have been sent, then shuts down the outgoing stream. The
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// returned promise resolves after shutdown is complete.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    fn shutdown(&mut self, result: ::capnp::Result<()>) -> Promise<(), Error>;
[188](https://docs.rs#188)}
[189](https://docs.rs#189)
[190](https://docs.rs#190)/// Tracks a particular RPC stream in order to implement a flow control algorithm.
[191](https://docs.rs#191)pub trait FlowController {
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    fn send(
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        &mut self,
[194](https://docs.rs#194)        message: Box<dyn OutgoingMessage>,
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        ack: Promise<(), Error>,
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    ) -> Promise<(), Error>;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    fn wait_all_acked(&mut self) -> Promise<(), Error>;
[198](https://docs.rs#198)}
[199](https://docs.rs#199)
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// Network facility between vats, it determines how to form connections between
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// vats.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)///
[203](https://docs.rs#203)/// ## Vat
[204](https://docs.rs#204)///
[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// Cap'n Proto RPC operates between vats, where a "vat" is some sort of host of
[206](https://docs.rs#206)/// objects.  Typically one Cap'n Proto process (in the Unix sense) is one vat.
[207](https://docs.rs#207)pub trait VatNetwork<VatId> {
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    /// Connects to `host_id`.
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    ///
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    /// Returns None if `host_id` refers to the local vat.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    fn connect(&mut self, host_id: VatId) -> Option<Box<dyn Connection<VatId>>>;
[212](https://docs.rs#212)
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// Waits for the next incoming connection and return it.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    fn accept(&mut self) -> Promise<Box<dyn Connection<VatId>>, ::capnp::Error>;
[215](https://docs.rs#215)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// A promise that cannot be resolved until the shutdown.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    fn drive_until_shutdown(&mut self) -> Promise<(), Error>;
[218](https://docs.rs#218)}
[219](https://docs.rs#219)
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// A portal to objects available on the network.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)///
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// The RPC implementation sits on top of an implementation of [`VatNetwork`], which
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// determines how to form connections between vats. The RPC implementation determines
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// how to use such connections to manage object references and make method calls.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)/// At the moment, this is all rather more general than it needs to be, because the only
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// implementation of `VatNetwork` is [`twoparty::VatNetwork`]. However, eventually we
[228](https://docs.rs#228)/// will need to have more sophisticated `VatNetwork` implementations, in order to support
[229](https://docs.rs#229)/// [level 3](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)///
[231](https://docs.rs#231)/// An `RpcSystem` is a non-`Send`able `Future` and needs to be driven by a task
[232](https://docs.rs#232)/// executor. A common way accomplish that is to pass the `RpcSystem` to
[233](https://docs.rs#233)/// `tokio::task::spawn_local()`.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)#[must_use = "futures do nothing unless polled"]
[235](https://docs.rs#235)pub struct RpcSystem<VatId>
[236](https://docs.rs#236)where
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    VatId: 'static,
[238](https://docs.rs#238){
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    network: Box<dyn crate::VatNetwork<VatId>>,
[240](https://docs.rs#240)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    bootstrap_cap: Box<dyn ClientHook>,
[242](https://docs.rs#242)
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    // XXX To handle three or more party networks, this should be a map from connection pointers
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    // to connection states.
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    connection_state: Rc<RefCell<Option<Rc<rpc::ConnectionState<VatId>>>>>,
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    tasks: TaskSet<Error>,
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    handle: crate::task_set::TaskSetHandle<Error>,
[249](https://docs.rs#249)}
[250](https://docs.rs#250)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)impl<VatId> RpcSystem<VatId> {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    /// Constructs a new `RpcSystem` with the given network and bootstrap capability.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    pub fn new(
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        mut network: Box<dyn crate::VatNetwork<VatId>>,
[255](https://docs.rs#255)        bootstrap: Option<::capnp::capability::Client>,
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    ) -> Self {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        let bootstrap_cap = match bootstrap {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)            Some(cap) => cap.hook,
[259](https://docs.rs#259)            None => broken::new_cap(Error::failed("no bootstrap capability".to_string())),
[260](https://docs.rs#260)        };
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        let (mut handle, tasks) = TaskSet::new(Box::new(SystemTaskReaper));
[262](https://docs.rs#262)
[263](https://docs.rs#263)        let mut handle1 = handle.clone();
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        handle.add(network.drive_until_shutdown().then(move |r| {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            let r = match r {
[266](https://docs.rs#266)                Ok(()) => Ok(()),
[267](https://docs.rs#267)                Err(e) => {
[268](https://docs.rs#268)                    if e.kind != ::capnp::ErrorKind::Disconnected {
[269](https://docs.rs#269)                        // Don't report disconnects as an error.
[270](https://docs.rs#270)                        Err(e)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)                    } else {
[272](https://docs.rs#272)                        Ok(())
[273](https://docs.rs#273)                    }
[274](https://docs.rs#274)                }
[275](https://docs.rs#275)            };
[276](https://docs.rs#276)
[277](https://docs.rs#277)            handle1.terminate(r);
[278](https://docs.rs#278)            Promise::ok(())
[279](https://docs.rs#279)        }));
[280](https://docs.rs#280)
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        let mut result = Self {
[282](https://docs.rs#282)            network,
[283](https://docs.rs#283)            bootstrap_cap,
[284](https://docs.rs#284)            connection_state: Rc::new(RefCell::new(None)),
[285](https://docs.rs#285)
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            tasks,
[287](https://docs.rs#287)            handle: handle.clone(),
[288](https://docs.rs#288)        };
[289](https://docs.rs#289)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        let accept_loop = result.accept_loop();
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        handle.add(accept_loop);
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        result
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    }
[294](https://docs.rs#294)
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    /// Connects to the given vat and returns its bootstrap interface, returns
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    /// a client that can be used to invoke the bootstrap interface.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    pub fn bootstrap<T>(&mut self, vat_id: VatId) -> T
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    where
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        T: ::capnp::capability::FromClientHook,
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)        let Some(connection) = self.network.connect(vat_id) else {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)            return T::new(self.bootstrap_cap.clone());
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        };
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        let connection_state = Self::get_connection_state(
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            &self.connection_state,
[306](https://docs.rs#306)            self.bootstrap_cap.clone(),
[307](https://docs.rs#307)            connection,
[308](https://docs.rs#308)            self.handle.clone(),
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        );
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        let hook = rpc::ConnectionState::bootstrap(&connection_state);
[312](https://docs.rs#312)        T::new(hook)
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    }
[314](https://docs.rs#314)
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    // not really a loop, because it doesn't need to be for the two party case
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    fn accept_loop(&mut self) -> Promise<(), Error> {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        let connection_state_ref = self.connection_state.clone();
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        let bootstrap_cap = self.bootstrap_cap.clone();
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        let handle = self.handle.clone();
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        Promise::from_future(self.network.accept().map_ok(move |connection| {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)            Self::get_connection_state(&connection_state_ref, bootstrap_cap, connection, handle);
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        }))
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    // If `connection_state_ref` is not already populated, populates it with a new
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    // `ConnectionState` built from a local bootstrap capability and `connection`,
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    // spawning any background tasks onto `handle`. Returns the resulting value
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    // held in `connection_state_ref`.
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    fn get_connection_state(
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        connection_state_ref: &Rc<RefCell<Option<Rc<rpc::ConnectionState<VatId>>>>>,
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        bootstrap_cap: Box<dyn ClientHook>,
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        connection: Box<dyn crate::Connection<VatId>>,
[333](https://docs.rs#333)        mut handle: crate::task_set::TaskSetHandle<Error>,
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    ) -> Rc<rpc::ConnectionState<VatId>> {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)        // TODO this needs to be updated once we allow more general VatNetworks.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        let (tasks, result) = match *connection_state_ref.borrow() {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)            Some(ref connection_state) => {
[338](https://docs.rs#338)                // return early.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                return connection_state.clone();
[340](https://docs.rs#340)            }
[341](https://docs.rs#341)            None => {
[342](https://docs.rs#342)                let (on_disconnect_fulfiller, on_disconnect_promise) =
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                    oneshot::channel::<Promise<(), Error>>();
[344](https://docs.rs#344)                let connection_state_ref1 = connection_state_ref.clone();
[345](https://docs.rs#345)                handle.add(on_disconnect_promise.then(move |shutdown_promise| {
[346](https://docs.rs#346)                    *connection_state_ref1.borrow_mut() = None;
[347](https://docs.rs#347)                    match shutdown_promise {
[348](https://docs.rs#348)                        Ok(s) => s,
[349](https://docs.rs#349)                        Err(e) => Promise::err(Error::failed(format!("{e}"))),
[350](https://docs.rs#350)                    }
[351](https://docs.rs#351)                }));
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                rpc::ConnectionState::new(bootstrap_cap, connection, on_disconnect_fulfiller)
[353](https://docs.rs#353)            }
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        };
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        *connection_state_ref.borrow_mut() = Some(result.clone());
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        handle.add(tasks);
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        result
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    }
[359](https://docs.rs#359)
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// Returns a `Disconnector` future that can be run to cleanly close the connection to this `RpcSystem`'s network.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// You should get the `Disconnector` before you spawn the `RpcSystem`.
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    pub fn get_disconnector(&self) -> rpc::Disconnector<VatId> {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)        rpc::Disconnector::new(self.connection_state.clone())
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    }

[435](https://docs.rs#435)    pub fn new_client_from_rc(&mut self, rc: Rc<S>) -> C {
[436](https://docs.rs#436)        let weak = Rc::downgrade(&rc);
[437](https://docs.rs#437)        let ptr = Rc::as_ptr(&rc) as usize;

[442](https://docs.rs#442)    }

[444](https://docs.rs#444)    /// Looks up a capability and returns its underlying server object, if found.
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    /// Fully resolves the capability before looking it up.
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    pub async fn get_local_server(&self, client: &C) -> Option<Rc<S>>
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    where
[448](https://docs.rs#448)        C: capnp::capability::FromClientHook,
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    {
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        let resolved: C = capnp::capability::get_resolved_cap(
[451](https://docs.rs#451)            capnp::capability::FromClientHook::new(client.as_client_hook().add_ref()),
[452](https://docs.rs#452)        )
[453](https://docs.rs#453)        .await;
[454](https://docs.rs#454)        let hook = resolved.into_client_hook();
[455](https://docs.rs#455)        let ptr = hook.get_ptr();
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        self.caps.get(&ptr).and_then(|c| c.upgrade())
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    }
[458](https://docs.rs#458)
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    /// Looks up a capability and returns its underlying server object, if found.
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// Does *not* attempt to resolve the capability first, so you will usually want
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    /// to call `get_resolved_cap()` before calling this. The advantage of this method

[463](https://docs.rs#463)    /// over a shorter span (which can be very important if `self` is inside a `RefCell`).

}## Expand description

Network facility between vats, it determines how to form connections between vats.

[§](https://docs.rs#vat)Vat

Cap’n Proto RPC operates between vats, where a “vat” is some sort of host of objects. Typically one Cap’n Proto process (in the Unix sense) is one vat.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

# pry in capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/macro.pry.html

```
macro_rules! pry {
    ($expr:expr) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Like [ try!()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.try.html), but for functions that return a

[rather than a](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/capability/struct.Promise.html)

`Promise<T, E>`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result<T, E>`Unwraps a `Result<T, E>`. In the case of an error `Err(e)`, immediately returns from the
enclosing function with `Promise::err(e)`.

# CapabilityServerSet in capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/struct.CapabilityServerSet.html

`pub struct CapabilityServerSet<S, C>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Collection of unwrappable capabilities.

Allows a server to recognize its own capabilities when passed back to it, and obtain the
underlying Server objects associated with them. Holds only weak references to Server objects
allowing Server objects to be dropped when dropped by the remote client. Call the `gc` method
to reclaim memory used for Server objects that have been dropped.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnp_rpc/lib.rs.html#464-471)#### pub fn [get_local_server_of_resolved](https://docs.rs#method.get_local_server_of_resolved)(&self, client: [&C](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Rc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/rc/struct.Rc.html)<S>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnp_rpc/lib.rs.html#464-471)

#### pub fn [get_local_server_of_resolved](https://docs.rs#method.get_local_server_of_resolved)(&self, client: [&C](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Rc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/rc/struct.Rc.html)<S>>

Looks up a capability and returns its underlying server object, if found.
Does *not* attempt to resolve the capability first, so you will usually want
to call `get_resolved_cap()` before calling this. The advantage of this method
over `get_local_server()` is that this one is synchronous and borrows `self`
over a shorter span (which can be very important if `self` is inside a `RefCell`).

# RpcSystem in capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/struct.RpcSystem.html

Struct RpcSystem  Copy item path  Source  `pub struct RpcSystem<VatId>`where
    VatId: 'static,

{  }Expand description A portal to objects available on the network.

The RPC implementation sits on top of an implementation of `VatNetwork`

At the moment, this is all rather more general than it needs to be, because the only
implementation of `VatNetwork` is `twoparty::VatNetwork``VatNetwork` implementations, in order to support
level 3  features.

An `RpcSystem` is a non-`Send`able `Future` and needs to be driven by a task
executor. A common way accomplish that is to pass the `RpcSystem` to
`tokio::task::spawn_local()`.

Constructs a new `RpcSystem` with the given network and bootstrap capability.

Connects to the given vat and returns its bootstrap interface, returns
a client that can be used to invoke the bootstrap interface.

Returns a `Disconnector` future that can be run to cleanly close the connection to this `RpcSystem`’s network.
You should get the `Disconnector` before you spawn the `RpcSystem`.

The type of value produced on completion.

Attempts to resolve the future to a final value, registering
the current task for wakeup if the value is not yet available.

Allocates a new message to be sent on this connection.

If `first_segment_word_size` is non-zero, it should be treated as a
hint suggesting how large to make the first segment.  This is entirely
a hint and the connection may adjust it up or down.  If it is zero,
the connection should choose the size itself.

Gets the total size of the message, for flow control purposes. Although the caller could also call get_body().target_size(), doing that would walk the message tree, whereas typical implementations can compute the size more cheaply by summing segment sizes.

# SetTarget in capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/trait.SetTarget.html

```
pub trait SetTarget<C> {
    // Required methods
    fn
```
[add_ref](https://docs.rs#tymethod.add_ref)(&self) -> [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [SetTarget](https://docs.rs/trait.SetTarget.html)<C>>;
[set_target](https://docs.rs#tymethod.set_target)(&self, target: C);
}## Expand description

Trait implemented by the reconnecting client to set new connection out-of-band.

When using [ auto_reconnect](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_reconnect.html) or

[it is not always optimal to wait for a call to fail with](https://docs.rs/fn.lazy_auto_reconnect.html)

`lazy_auto_reconnect`[before replacing the client that is wrapped with a new fresh one.](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected)

`Disconnected`Sometimes we know by other means that a client has gone away. It could be that we have clients that automatically sends us a new capability when it reconnects to us.

For these situations you can use the implementation of this trait that you get from
[ auto_reconnect](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_reconnect.html) or

[to manually set the target of the wrapped client.](https://docs.rs/fn.lazy_auto_reconnect.html)

`lazy_auto_reconnect`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// The reconnecting client that automatically calls connect
let (foo_client, set_target) = auto_reconnect(|| {
    Ok(new_future_client(connect()))
})?;
// do work with foo_client
...
// We become aware that the client has gone so reconnect manually
set_target.set_target(new_future_client(connect()));
// do more work with foo_client
...
```

# auto_reconnect in capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/fn.auto_reconnect.html

## Expand description

Creates a new client that reconnects when getting [ ErrorKind::Disconnected](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected) errors.

Usually when you get a [ Disconnected](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected) error response from calling a method on a capability
it means the end of that capability for good. And so you can’t call methods on that
capability any more.

When you have a way of getting the capability back: Be it from a bootstrap or because
the capability is persistent this method can help you wrap that reconnection logic into a client
that automatically runs the logic whenever a method call returns [ Disconnected](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected).

The way it works is that you provide a closure that returns a fresh client or a permanent error and
you get a new connected client and a [ SetTarget](https://docs.rs/trait.SetTarget.html) interface that you can optionally use to prematurely
replace the client.

There is one caveat though: The original request that got a [ Disconnected](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected)
will still get that response. It is up to the caller to retry the call if relevant. `auto_reconnect`` only
deals with the calls that come after.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
# Cap'n Proto schema
interface Foo {
    identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// A simple bootstrapped tcp connection to remote.example.com
async fn connect() -> capnp::Result<foo_client::Client> {
    let stream = tokio::net::TcpStream::connect(&"remote.example.com:3001").await?;
    stream.set_nodelay(true)?;
    let (reader, writer) = tokio_util::compat::TokioAsyncReadCompatExt::compat(stream).split();
    let network = Box::new(twoparty::VatNetwork::new(
        futures::io::BufReader::new(reader),
        futures::io::BufWriter::new(writer),
        rpc_twoparty_capnp::Side::Client,
        Default::default(),
    ));
    let mut rpc_system = RpcSystem::new(network, None);
    let foo_client: foo_client::Client = rpc_system.bootstrap(rpc_twoparty_capnp::Side::Server);
    tokio::task::spawn_local(rpc_system);
    Ok(foo_client)
}
// The reconnecting client that automatically calls connect
let (foo_client, _) = auto_reconnect(|| {
    // By using new_future_client we delay any calls until we have a new connection.
    Ok(new_future_client(connect()))
})?;
// Calling Foo like normally.
let mut request = foo_client.identity_request();
request.get().set_x(123);
let promise = request.send().promise.and_then(|response| {
    println!("results = {}", response.get()?.get_y());
    Ok(())
});
```
